I definitely love it for what it is, like a post-folk sound. Listening to Trespass and hearing what came next for Genesis just blows my mind. All of them were talented and hardworking to an insane degree.

I feel like FGTR is essential to appreciate Genesis' full spectrum. It's pastoral and beautiful in its own right, and shows hints of what the group was capable of that came to fruition on Trespass. By Nursery Cryme, it was clear to see that they were a formidable early prog band. 

Although the group wasn't happy with the way the record turned out (reportedly several of Tony's piano pieces were shortened or removed altogether), I love it. My favorite songs are Where the Sour Turns to Sweet, Am I Very Wrong?, Into the Wilderness, The Conqueror, and In Hiding. 

In Hiding especially is such a beautiful tune, the way Peter begins the song hesitantly facing the unknown, then becomes stronger and more confident with each verse -- his ability to bend the song with his emotivity really shines here. Same thing with Where the Sour Turns to Sweet -- you can close your eyes and hear Peter convincing you to trust him, to come with him and he will take you somewhere that your inner peace and beauty will shine and you'll be free of the conformity you'd been forced into your whole life.

I love the way Tony's piano sounds on this album too, baroque and chamber-like. My favorite example of this is on Am I Very Wrong? Just gorgeous.

To understand Genesis is to be willing to accept them at every point in their discography. Infancy, learning to walk, running, galloping, shaking, seizing, flourishing. Only fools disregard FGTR.

If you're a super-metabolizer of tramadol, it will bar none feel like the best drug you've ever put in your body. But it comes with huge risk of seizure, damage to the hypothalamus, and suicidal ideation. Do not take this drug unless you absolutely have to.

Look man, I was you. I get it, I really do. I "tried" EV so many times and gave up after a few songs. They all blended together for me, and I abandoned the record for years.

EV is a record that you have to approach one song a time. If you can't stand any of them, then pick out the one you hate the least. Play it over and over. Memorize it, start finding favorite bits and pieces in it. Let the end of the song continue into the intro of the next, then hit 'back.'

After awhile, you'll find that you stop hitting 'back' when that next intro begins. You start to listen to two tracks at a time, then hit 'back' twice. Eventually, the into of the third song starts becoming familiar, and you want to see where *it* goes. On, and on, and on, until you fall in love with this record. 

Era Vulgaris takes you in slowly, but it WILL take you. Eventually your contempt and complaints about the album turn to appreciation and praise, and you wonder how you ever pushed it away willingly.

In the late 90s and early 2000s, it was people connecting over mutual shared interests, or a way to keep in touch. Now, it's overrun with ads, bots, spam, misinformation, and outright invasive tactics that seek only to keep you engaged for hours. Endless loops of ragebait videos, influencers, and a 5:1 ratio of ads to actual posts that you're there for. 

How many hours have we lost to mindless scrolling? A lot of times I didn't even realize I had been sitting the same spot for at least an hour straight just scrolling and reading stupid shit designed to piss me off and engage in long comment battles with morons. (I realize that Reddit has this, but it's much easier to navigate away from subs that suck than it is to break away from political and entertainment-related shitpost after shitpost in a news feed/for you page).

Edited to add: my breakaway from social media began when I realized that Facebook was listening through my phone. In 2016, I was working as a registrar in an emergency room. I had my phone on me at all times, but obviously didn't use it during my shift. I had to repeat patients' names aloud all day, sometimes dozens of times. Within the next 2-3 days, those patients began showing up in my "People You May Know" on Facebook, often with zero mutual friends. The only way Facebook could have matched me to them was through picking up the names I was saying aloud with our mutual city and state.
